submission.natural_language_explanation: N1845+ is an evaluative-significance detector: it fires on the word that carries the text's assessment of how much something matters - how valuable, costly, risky, important, difficult, easy, dangerous, useful, likely, good or bad it is - whether that word is an evaluative or modal adjective ('important' 1.85, 'impossible' 2.11, 'difficult' 1.76, 'dangerous' 1.83, 'useful' 1.43, 'beautiful' 1.21, 'amazing' 1.61, 'obvious' 1.47) or a significance noun ('value', 'cost', 'risk', 'benefit', 'mortality' 1.16), and it peaks highest when a degree word puts that assessment on a scale ('as important as' 1.85, 'much more dangerous than' 1.73, 'nearly impossible' 2.07), while sitting at the negative floor on descriptive or classificatory words that carry no such judgement - colour, shape, material and taste ('blue' 0.12, 'round' -0.09, 'wooden' 0.11, 'salty' 0.33) - which also rules out a rarity/surprisal reading ('crimson' 0.33, 'rectangular' 0.02 against 'useful' 1.31). The copula is not the detected feature: 'The church was ___' gives an identical 0.58 on 'was' whatever the predicate, so the 'is/was/were' peaks in the scan reflect this pole's flat per-token response, not its content.

Pitching the tent takes about twenty minutes. Start by laying the groundsheet flat, green side down, with the rectangular footprint centred on the flattest part of the shelf. The bag holds three aluminium poles, each in a separate sleeve, and a folded flysheet of blue nylon.

Unroll the inner tent and lay it along the long axis of the groundsheet. The pole sleeves run corner to corner in a shallow curve; feed the first pole through the sleeve from the left corner until its tip shows at the far end. Repeat with the second pole along the other diagonal, then with the third across the middle.

Push each pole tip into the brass eyelet at its corner. The frame will rise on its own once all six eyelets are seated. Clip the four plastic hooks under the crossing points, working from the middle outward so the fabric sits without slack.

Peg out the corners first: two pegs at the head end, two at the foot, each set at forty-five degrees to the ground and driven until the hook sits flush. Then the two side loops, then the loop midway along each wall. The guy lines are stored in the pocket by the door, coiled and tied with a short length of cord.

Drape the flysheet over the frame with the darker panel at the head end and the seam over the ridge. The flysheet corners have short elastic loops; hook them to the pegs already in place and add the two spare pegs at the middle of the long sides. The gap between fly and inner should be a hand's width at the foot.

The door has two panels, each with a mesh screen behind it. Roll the outer panel back and tie it at the side. Peg the threshold groundsheet to the last two loops, then check the line of the ridge: it should run straight between the head and foot poles.

Finally, push the valve open on the groundsheet and lay the pump beside it. Two of the pegs are bent at the top and belong at the corners; the straight ones go along the sides. The whole kit weighs four kilograms and packs into a bag about the size of a shoebox.

The instruction card is stitched into the inside of the bag. It shows the pole layout as a simple diagram, with the doors marked in red and the vents in grey, and a table of the pegs by size. If the wind picks up overnight, the two lines at the head end can be doubled back to the pegs at the corners, and the vent flap left closed.

The bridge carries the old coach road over the river about a mile west of the village, on three stone arches with a brick parapet added in 1889. Traffic has run on it, with brief interruptions, since the 1750s, and the county ordered a survey after the winter floods undercut the western bank.

The engineers worked from a floating platform for nine days, sounding the piers and photographing each arch from both faces. Their report runs to sixty pages and describes the masonry course by course: the spandrels, the coping stones, the patched section of parapet above the second arch, the drain outlets at the base of each pier.

The central finding is that the eastern pier has settled by nineteen millimetres since the last inspection in 2011, and that the two visible cracks in the arch ring have widened by about three millimetres. The surveyors judged the damage severe enough to justify restricting heavy vehicles to a single lane, and they recommended that the repairs be treated as urgent.

The rest of the document is technical. It records the depth of the scour hole on the downstream side, the condition of the timber fenders, the composition of the mortar sampled at four points, and the sequence of repairs carried out after the 1998 flood, when a section of the western parapet was rebuilt in a harder brick than the original.

Boreholes were sunk at six locations, three on each bank, to a depth of eight metres. The cores show a layer of river gravel over clay, with the pier footings resting on the gravel at about four metres.

The report also sets out three options for the work, ranging from repointing and scour protection to a full rebuild of the eastern arch. The rebuild would require a temporary bailey bridge beside the site and the closure of the road for most of a year, and at an estimated forty-one thousand hours of labour it would be far more expensive than the other two options combined.

Copies of the survey were placed in the parish library and the district office in March, and public comment was invited for six weeks. Nineteen responses were received, most of them from residents of the two farms on the western side, who wrote about school buses, the milk lorry and the diversion that would add eleven miles to any journey into town.

explanation_scores.explanation: N1845+ is an evaluative-significance detector: it fires on the word that carries the text's assessment of how much something matters - how valuable, costly, risky, important, difficult, easy, dangerous, useful, likely, good or bad it is - whether that word is an evaluative or modal adjective ('important' 1.85, 'impossible' 2.11, 'difficult' 1.76, 'dangerous' 1.83, 'useful' 1.43, 'beautiful' 1.21, 'amazing' 1.61, 'obvious' 1.47) or a significance noun ('value', 'cost', 'risk', 'benefit', 'mortality' 1.16), and it peaks highest when a degree word puts that assessment on a scale ('as important as' 1.85, 'much more dangerous than' 1.73, 'nearly impossible' 2.07), while sitting at the negative floor on descriptive or classificatory words that carry no such judgement - colour, shape, material and taste ('blue' 0.12, 'round' -0.09, 'wooden' 0.11, 'salty' 0.33) - which also rules out a rarity/surprisal reading ('crimson' 0.33, 'rectangular' 0.02 against 'useful' 1.31). The copula is not the detected feature: 'The church was ___' gives an identical 0.58 on 'was' whatever the predicate, so the 'is/was/were' peaks in the scan reflect this pole's flat per-token response, not its content.
